data.content_ref: inline:The target's own mechanism refutes its central claim. It frames the preference as 'a bet on the currently fittest survivor,' and justifies choosing the better-corroborated theory 'because it has proven itself the most robust instrument for survival and problem-solving so far.' A 'bet' is inherently forward-looking: it is an action taken on the expectation of a future payoff. To justify that bet by citing past performance ('proven itself... so far') is the precise structure of inductive reasoning — using observed past regularity as the rational basis for expecting future success. The target cannot escape this by retreating to 'action, not belief,' because a bet that is rational requires a reason to expect the bet to pay off, and the only reason offered is past survival. This directly triggers the target's own countercondition: 'If the preference implies any increase in subjective probability or rational expectation of future success, it collapses into induction.' The evolutionary analogy fails to rescue the argument because natural selection is a retrospective explanatory mechanism (it explains why current survivors exist), whereas the scientist's preference is a prospective choice. Organisms do not 'prefer' fitness — they merely survive. Conflating retrospective selection with prospective choice smuggles induction in through the very concept of a 'bet.'
